rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dividing bodies into subtle and dense does not prove that all bodies share a common essence, just as dividing accidents into quality and quantity does not establish shared essential properties.
rows.anchor: يمكن تقسيم العرض إلى الكيف والكم ولم يلزم أن يكون هناك قدر مشترك من الذاتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A subtle airy body could differ essentially from other air, with its nature entailing distinctive knowledge and extraordinary power; this makes jinn and their ability to assume forms plausible.
rows.anchor: لا يمتنع في بعض الأجسام اللطيفة الهوائية أن تكون مخالفة لسائر أنواع الهواء في الماهية

rows.speaker: الأشعري وجمهور أتباعه
rows.claim: Al-Ashʿarī and most followers deny that bodily structure is a condition for life.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الأشعري وجمهور أتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their argument is that one life cannot inhere simultaneously in many substrates; if each equal part had its own life, dependence between the parts would create a circle, so an individual part can live independently.
rows.anchor: والأول محال لأن حلول العرض الواحد في المحال الكثيرة دفعة واحدة غير معقول

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites argue that structure is necessary because life disappears when the structure breaks down and remains while it stays intact.
rows.anchor: وأما دليل المعتزلة وهو أنه لا بد من البنية فليس إلا الاستقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects that induction as proof of necessity: observed cases do not establish the state of unobserved cases, and the inference assumes that miracles cannot break ordinary patterns.
rows.anchor: فإن الاستقراء لا يفيد القطع بالوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since life need not depend on structure, God can give an individual atom knowledge and power for difficult acts, making jinn possible whether their bodies are subtle or dense and their parts large or small.
rows.anchor: أن يخلق الله تعالى في الجوهر الفرد علما بأمور كثيرة

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ashʿarī permits a present visible object to go unperceived even when the sense is sound, conditions are met, and obstacles are absent; the Muʿtazilites deem this rationally impossible.
rows.anchor: أما الأشعري وأتباعه فقد جوزوه ، وأما المعتزلة فقد حكموا بامتناعه عقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distant large object appears small because only some of its parts are seen, though the perceptual conditions apply equally to unseen parts; perception is therefore not necessary when conditions obtain.
rows.anchor: أنا نرى الكبير من البعد صغيرا وما ذاك إلا أنا نرى بعض أجزاء ذلك البعيد دون البعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If seeing one part depends on seeing another, equal parts produce circular dependence; if not, an atom could be seen alone, though an isolated atom is not seen, showing perception is possible rather than necessary.
rows.anchor: فإما أن تكون رؤية هذا الجزء مشروطة برؤية ذلك الجزء الآخر أو لا تكون

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites object that allowing nonperception under adequate conditions would mean nearby drums and horns might not be seen or heard.
rows.anchor: أما المعتزلة فقد عولوا على أنا لو جوزنا ذلك لجوزنا أن يكون بحضرتنا طبلات وبوقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says this objection leaves no principled distinction between regular habits and necessities: the same reasoning would permit seas turning to gold, mountains to jewels, or extra suns appearing unseen.
rows.anchor: والسبب في هذا التشوش أن هؤلاء المعتزلة نظروا إلى هذه الأمور المطردة في مناهج العادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says one must treat all such events alike, either as necessary as the philosophers do or as nonnecessary as al-Ashʿarī does; an arbitrary split is untenable.
rows.anchor: بل الواجب أن يسوى بين الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Ashʿarī’s account, jinn may be powerful, dense bodies yet remain unseen even while present.
rows.anchor: فإن أجسامهم وإن كانت كثيفة قوية إلا أنه يمتنع أن لا تراها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān says angels and jinn can perform difficult acts, which would require dense, solid organs on the Muʿtazilite premise; angels attend people, the Prophet, and the dying without being seen.
rows.anchor: على أن للملائكة قوة عظيمة على الأفعال الشاقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If powerful angels and jinn are subtle, that contradicts the claim that subtle bodies cannot do hard work; if they are dense, their frequent presence without being seen contradicts the Muʿtazilite view of perception.
rows.anchor: وإن قالوا : إنها أجسام لطيفة وحية ، ولكنها للطافتها لا تقدر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet did not see the jinn: after heaven was guarded and meteors drove them away, investigators reached Tihāma, heard the Prophet reciting at dawn in ʿUkāẓ, recognized the cause, and returned to warn their people.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب ابن عباس أنه عليه السلام ما رآهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās infers that the Prophet had not seen them because, had he witnessed the event, he would not have attributed his knowledge of it to revelation.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل على أنه عليه السلام لم ير الجن إذ لو رآهم لما أسند معرفة هذه الواقعة إلى الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconciliation is that jinn were accompanying the devils when the latter were struck by meteors while spying on heaven.
rows.anchor: فيه وجهان الأول : أن الجن كانوا مع الشياطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the ones struck by meteors were themselves jinn, called devils because a shayṭān is any rebellious being far from obedience to God.
rows.anchor: الثاني : أن الذين رموا بالشهب كانوا من الجن

rows.speaker: عاصم عن ذر
rows.claim: A report from ʿĀṣim via Dharr identifies the visitors as a group led by Zawbaʿa and his companions, who heard the Prophet recite in Mecca and returned; Rāzī links this to 46:29.
rows.anchor: روى عاصم عن ذر قال : قدم رهط زوبعة وأصحابه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as the Shayṣabān, the most numerous jinn and the main body of Iblīs’s troops.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كانوا من الشيصبان وهم أكثر الجن عددا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet was ordered to go to the jinn and recite the Qurʾān; he accompanied him to al-Ḥajūn, where a throng of jinn gathered, heard the recitation, and remained unseen to him.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب ابن مسعود أنه أمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالمسير إليهم ليقرأ القرآن عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: In another version, the jinn ask who the Prophet is and for a witness; a tree comes, testifies that he is God’s Messenger, then returns to its place.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أخرى فقالوا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ما أنت

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The jinn later ask for provisions, and the Prophet gives them bones and dung; he forbids people to use either as food.
rows.anchor: فسألوني الزاد فزودتهم العظم والبعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the reports about Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd cannot be rejected and offers several ways to reconcile them.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه لا سبيل إلى تكذيب الروايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The event Ibn ʿAbbās describes may have happened first, with revelation of this sūra, followed later by the Prophet’s instructed visit described by Ibn Masʿūd.
rows.anchor: لعل ما ذكره ابن عباس وقع أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If there was one event, the Prophet may have visited and recited without knowing what the jinn said or did, and God then revealed it to him.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه عليه السلام ما عرف أنهم ماذا قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the Prophet saw and heard the believing jinn; after they returned and told their people what had happened, God revealed their account to him.
rows.anchor: وهو عليه السلام رآهم وسمع كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “Say” tells the Prophet to disclose to his companions what God revealed about the jinn episode; Rāzī lists its benefits: the Prophet’s mission includes jinn, Quraysh see the Qurʾān’s inimitability, jinn are morally responsible, understand human speech, and believing jinn call their kin to faith.
rows.anchor: وفيه فوائد إحداها : أن يعرفوا بذلك أنه عليه السلام كما بعث إلى الإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wahy is the discreet casting of meaning into the soul, as inspiration or an angel’s descent, and is done rapidly.
rows.anchor: الإيحاء إلقاء المعنى إلى النفس في خفاء كالإلهام وإنزال الملك

rows.speaker: يونس وهرون عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: The common reading is awḥā with an alif; Yūnus and Hārūn report that Abū ʿAmr read waḥā with ḍamma on wāw and no alif.
rows.anchor: القراءة المشهورة ، { أوحى } بالألف

rows.speaker: قُرِىء
rows.claim: Another reading is aḥyā, with hamza instead of the original wāw, by analogy with aʿada and azana.
rows.anchor: وقرىء { * أحي } بالهمز من غير واو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They agree that anna in “that a group of jinn listened” takes fatḥ because the clause is the passive subject of awḥā; Rāzī compares 6:19.
rows.anchor: أجمعوا على أن قوله : { أنه استمع } بالفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They agree on kasr for innā in “we heard,” since it begins a quoted independent clause after the verb of saying.
rows.anchor: وأجمعوا على كسر إنا في قوله : { إنا سمعنا } لأنه مبتدأ محكي بعد القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading pattern gives fatḥ to clauses that belong to revelation and kasr to the jinn’s speech; the final clauses about mosques and the Prophet’s standing are exceptions to the jinn’s speech.
rows.anchor: فما كان من الوحي فتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second pattern opens all the following clauses by supplying “we believed in it and believed that…,” including the claims about the Lord’s greatness and the fool’s speech.
rows.anchor: وثانيهما : فتح الكل والتقدير : فآمنا به وآمنا بأنه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This second parsing faces two objections: attaching belief to clauses such as “our fool used to say” sounds improper, and Arabic does not coordinate onto a genitive pronoun without repeating the preposition.
rows.anchor: أحدهما : أنه يقبح إضافة الإيمان إلى بعض هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that taking āmannā to mean “we affirmed and testified” resolves both objections.
rows.anchor: والجواب : عن الإشكالين أنا إذا حملنا قوله : آمنا على معنى صدقنا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarites cite “that We may test them” as evidence that God leads His servants astray.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا بقوله : { لنفتنهم } على أنه تعالى يضل عباده

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites answer that fitna means testing, as gold is tested in fire, rather than creating misguidance.
rows.anchor: والمعتزلة أجابوا بأن الفتنة هي الاختبار كما يقال : فتنت الذهب بالنار

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer from the purpose lām that God acts for an end.
rows.anchor: واستدلت المعتزلة باللام في قوله { لنفتنهم } على أنه تعالى

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarites answer that, by agreement, the testing itself is not an intended purpose, so this verse shows the lām does not express a divine purpose.
rows.anchor: وأصحابنا أجابوا أن الفتنة بالاتفاق ليست مقصودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away from the remembrance of one’s Lord can mean turning away from worship, admonition, or revelation.
rows.anchor: أي عن عبادته أو عن موعظته

rows.speaker: قُرِىء
rows.claim: The verb is also read with nūn, either fatḥa or ḍamma, meaning “We make him enter” a punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرىء بالنون مفتوحة ومضمومة أي ندخله عذابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying phrase is “We make him enter into a punishment”; the preposition may be omitted and the verb made transitive, as in 7:155, or the verb may itself mean “make enter.”
rows.anchor: والأصل نسلكه في عذاب كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿad is a verbal noun of ṣaʿida and describes punishment that rises over the punished person and overwhelms him beyond his capacity.
rows.anchor: والصعد مصدر صعد ، يقال

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar said nothing overwhelmed him as much as the marriage sermon, using taṣʿad to mean that something weighed on or overcame him.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول عمر : ما تصعدني شيء ما تصعدتني خطبة النكاح

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from ʿIkrima via Ibn ʿAbbās says ṣaʿad is a smooth rock in Hell: the unbeliever climbs it for forty years, is dragged back down, and must climb again forever.
rows.anchor: وهو ما روي عن عكرمة عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أن صعدا جبل في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī links this punishment to 74:17, “I shall make him undergo a steep ascent.”
rows.anchor: ونظير هذه الآية قوله تعالى : { سأرهقه صعودا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing is “It was revealed to me that the mosques belong to God.”
rows.anchor: التقدير : قل أوحي إلي أن المساجد لله

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl supplies an omitted lām: “because the mosques belong to God, do not invoke anyone with Him”; the prohibition applies in mosques, which belong exclusively to God.
rows.anchor: ومذهب الخليل أن التقدير : ولأن المساجد لله فلا تدعوا

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most interpreters take mosques as places built for prayer and remembrance, including synagogues, churches, and Muslim mosques; because People of the Book associate partners in their worship there, Muslims are commanded to worship sincerely and affirm God’s oneness.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الأكثرين : أنها المواضع التي بنيت للصلاة وذكر الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also interprets mosques as all places on earth, citing the Prophet’s statement that the earth was made a place of prostration; the earth belongs to God, so one should not prostrate on it to another.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : أراد بالمساجد البقاع كلها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan gives another interpretation: mosques are the prayers, with masājid as the plural of masjid, a verbal noun meaning prostration.
rows.anchor: روي عن الحسن أيضا أنه قال : المساجد هي الصلوات

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says mosques are the seven bodily members used in prostration: the feet, knees, hands, and face; they belong to God and should not be used to prostrate to another.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير : المساجد الأعضاء التي يسجد العبد عليها

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī selects Saʿīd ibn Jubayr’s interpretation of mosques as the body parts on which one prostrates.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول اختيار ابن الأنباري

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the mosques mean Mecca with all its mosques, since it is the world’s qibla and everyone turns toward it in prostration.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : يريد بالمساجد مكة

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says the singular is masjid with fatḥ in all interpretations except purpose-built prayer places, whose singular has kasr; he lists المسجد، المطلع، المنسك، المسكن، المنبت، المفرق، المسقط، المجزر، المحشر، المشرق، المغرب as exceptions, though fatḥ is permissible in all.
rows.anchor: وواحد المساجد على الأقوال كلها مسجد بفتح

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says it is sunna for a man entering a mosque to say “There is no god but God,” since the prohibition on invoking anyone with God implicitly commands remembering and calling upon Him.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : من السنة إذا دخل الرجل المسجد أن يقول لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree that “the servant of God” means the Prophet Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن عبدالله هو النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قول الجميع

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says this clause is the jinn’s speech rather than revelation, since the Messenger would not naturally speak about himself in the third person; Rāzī says this is possible and compares 19:85.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : إن هذا من كلام الجن لا من جملة الموحى

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most interpreters treat the clause as part of the revelation; otherwise non-jinn speech would interrupt the jinn’s words and damage the composition.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على أنه من جملة الموحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammatical choice tracks the interpretation: the initial hamza is open if the clause is revelation and kasr if it is the jinn’s speech.
rows.anchor: أن من جعله من جملة الموحى فتح الهمزة في أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If this is revelation and “they” means the jinn, the Prophet stood worshipping at dawn when they arrived; they nearly crowded over one another around him, amazed by his worship and the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: أحدها : إلى الجن ، ومعنى { قام يدعوه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes “they” the polytheists, who nearly crowded around the Prophet because he worshipped one God instead of their idols and they combined against him.
rows.anchor: والثاني : لما قدم رسول الله يعبد الله وحده

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says humans and jinn massed together against the Prophet to defeat the truth and extinguish God’s light, but God resolved to support and exalt him.
rows.anchor: وهو قول قتادة : لما قام عبدالله تلبدت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the clause is the jinn’s speech, the first two explanations of who nearly crowded around the Prophet can also apply.
rows.anchor: وأما على قول من قال : إنه من كلام الجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Libadan is the plural of libda, something matted and piled on itself; the same root describes tightly stuck material, rugs, and the matted mane behind a lion’s shoulders.
rows.anchor: فهو جمع لبدة وهو ما تلبد بعضه على بعض

rows.speaker: قُرِىء
rows.claim: The word is read with ḍamma on lām as lubada, equivalent in meaning to libda; other readings treat it as the plural of lābid or of lubūd.
rows.anchor: وقرىء : { لبدا } بضم اللام واللبدة في معنى اللبدة

rows.speaker: قُرِىء
rows.claim: A further reading has ḍamma on both lām and bāʾ and treats lubada as the plural of lubūd, like ṣubar as the plural of ṣabūr.
rows.anchor: وقرىء أيضا : { لبدا } بضم اللام والباء جمع لبود كصبر جمع صبور

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s line describes a lion with a mane whose claws have not been trimmed, using libd for the matted mane.
rows.anchor: لدى أسد شاكي السلاح مقذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling himself “the servant of God” suits the Prophet’s humility if the words are revelation; if they are the jinn’s, the point is that disbelievers tried to stop someone worshipping God, which accords with reason.
rows.anchor: لأنه إن كان هذا الكلام من جملة الموحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They unanimously identify the person meant as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.
rows.anchor: أجمعوا على أن المراد ههنا الوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parse makes waḥīdan an accusative circumstantial expression referring to God: “Leave me alone with him; I suffice to take vengeance on him.”
rows.anchor: أنه نصب على الحال ، ثم يحتمل أن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the circumstantial expression refers to God, it can mean that God created al-Walīd alone, with no partner in creation.
rows.anchor: خلقته وحدي لم يشركني في خلقه أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If it refers to al-Walīd, it means that God created him initially alone, without wealth or children, as in 6:94.
rows.anchor: وأما كونه حالا من المخلوق ، فعلى معنى أني خلقته حال ما كان وحيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parse treats waḥīdan as an accusative of disparagement: the verse addresses al-Walīd by the boastful nickname al-Waḥīd, which he used for himself and his father.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أنه نصب على الذم

rows.speaker: كثير من المتأخرين
rows.claim: Many later scholars object that this reading would make God affirm al-Walīd’s claim that he was unique and without equal.
rows.anchor: وطعن كثير من المتأخرين في هذا الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects that objection: al-Waḥīd may be a proper name rather than a quality, just as the condemned person in 44:49 is called “the mighty, the noble.”
rows.anchor: أنا لما جعلنا الوحيد اسم علم فقد زال السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reply is that al-Walīd may be called unique only in his own belief, as illustrated by 44:49.
rows.anchor: لم لا يجوز أن يحمل على كونه وحيدا في ظنه واعتقاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reply is that “unique” does not specify high rank; al-Walīd is unique only in disbelief, vileness, and lowliness.
rows.anchor: أن لفظ الوحيد ليس فيه أنه وحيد في العلو والشرف

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الضرير
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Ḍarīr parses waḥīdan as the second object of “created” and defines al-waḥīd as one without a father, casting doubt on al-Walīd’s lineage, as in 68:13.
rows.anchor: أن وحيدا مفعول ثان لخلق

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar explains extended wealth as a continuing inflow, arriving month after month.
rows.anchor: فلذلك فسره عمر بن الخطاب بغلة شهر شهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another meaning is wealth continually extended by increase, such as livestock, crops, and kinds of trade.
rows.anchor: أنه المال الذي يمد بالزيادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes al-Walīd’s wealth as physically extensive from Mecca to al-Ṭāʾif: camels, horses, sheep, many gardens, trees, rivers, and abundant money.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : كان ماله ممدودا ما بين مكة إلى الطائف

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says al-Walīd had a garden whose benefit never stopped in winter or summer; extended here means unending, as with the extended shade in 56:30.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : كان له بستان لا ينقطع نفعه شتاء ولا صيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is simply abundant wealth, whose enumeration would extend at length.
rows.anchor: أنه المال الكثير وذلك لأن المال الكثير إذا عدد فإنه يمتد تعديده

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators estimate it at one thousand dinars, others at four thousand, and others at one million.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم : ألف دينار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī dismisses these numerical estimates as arbitrary guesses that sound judgment does not favor.
rows.anchor: وهذه التحكمات مما لا يميل إليها الطبع السليم
